title: FP8/INT8 Sprint Results Summary (Draft) — Baseline vs Optimized
content:
Slide 1 — Title
FP8/INT8 Kernel Benchmarking Sprint — Results Summary (Draft)
Baseline vs Optimized • Tradeoffs • Recommended Defaults
Owners: Runtime Kernels + Runtime Scheduling + Bench Harness

Speaker notes:
- This deck is internal + draft. Numbers are from perf-lab runs pinned to the sprint runtime build and benchmark harness matrix.
- Focus is hosted traffic shapes (prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy), not pure microbench.


Slide 2 — Executive summary (what changed)
What we shipped/landed (or ready to land behind knobs):
- FP8 attention kernel tuning for H100/H200 (tile/launch config): +decode throughput, lower kernel time variance
- INT8 GEMM path: reduced conversion overhead, fused dequant in hot path where safe
- KV-cache interaction: avoid redundant scale/zero-point conversions in decode loop (quantized path)
- Scheduler: batch-size cap override for quantized decode to reduce tail latency under mixed prompt lengths
- Fix: FP8 prefill long-context alignment bug (correctness + perf stability)
- Logging/attribution: kernel-selection + quant-mode spans (guarded) + structured perf events for ingestion

Net outcome (across top hosted chat workloads):
- FP8: improved p95 TPOT and tokens/sec on H100/H200; TTFT mostly unchanged (scheduler dominates)
- INT8: improved cost proxy + tokens/sec on A100 and L40S; tail-latency improved with scheduler cap
- Correctness guardrails: drift checks added for INT8/FP8 vs FP16 baselines on a small prompt set

Speaker notes:
- “Optimized” = sprint runtime commit range including PRs 10622/10623/10624/10628/10630.
- End-to-end results depend heavily on workload (prefill vs decode) and scheduler settings.


Slide 3 — Scope / matrix (what these numbers represent)
Models (representative top-hosted families):
- Llama-family chat (8B/70B class proxy configs)
- Qwen-family chat
- Mistral-family chat

Hardware:
- A100 80GB
- H100 80GB
- H200 141GB (limited nodes; fewer repeats)
- L40S 48GB

Workloads:
- Streaming chat E2E: TTFT + TPOT + tokens/sec + queue wait time
- Prompt distributions: short (<=512), medium (~2k), long context (8k–16k) buckets
- Concurrency presets: low/med/high (traffic-shape-driven), mixed prompt lengths enabled

Quant modes compared:
- FP16 baseline
- FP8 (format per ADR; see notes on e4m3/e5m2)
- INT8 (weight-only + activation quant where supported by model/profile)

Speaker notes:
- We report deltas against FP16 baseline on the same GPU, same runtime build target, same harness config.
- For H200 we have fewer samples; treat numbers as directional until infra capacity improves.


Slide 4 — Methodology highlights (why we trust the deltas)
Pinned environment:
- Container digests pinned (bench harness + runtime build)
- GPU clocks/power: locked where allowed; otherwise recorded and tagged
- Warmup: fixed warmup iterations and pre-run cache fill

Stats:
- Each cell: N=20 runs (A100/H100/L40S), N=10 runs (H200)
- Outlier handling: robust comparator (median-of-means) + explicit “noisy run” flag
- Primary aggregation: p50/p95 for TTFT/TPOT; tokens/sec mean + CI; queue wait p95

Reliability caveats:
- L40S showed intermittent correctness failures with a fused op variant; reverted/disabled conditionally
- Perf-lab contention still shows up as queue wait spikes; scheduler isolation work ongoing

Speaker notes:
- Comparator improvements are in perf-canary/pr_189; we used the same logic for report tables.
- The dashboard tags include GPU clocks and node-id so we can audit drift.


Slide 5 — Definitions (TTFT, TPOT, cost proxy)
TTFT (ms):
- Time from request start to first token delivered (streaming)
- Includes queue wait + prefill + scheduler overhead

TPOT (ms/token):
- Time per output token after first token (streaming)
- Dominated by decode kernels + KV-cache + batching effects

Throughput (tokens/sec):
- Aggregate output tokens/sec for the run (includes batching behavior)

Cost proxy:
- GPU-ms per 1K output tokens (lower is better)
- Used internally for “cost-per-token” comparison across runs on same GPU SKU

Speaker notes:
- Cost proxy is not billing cost; it’s a stable internal metric for optimization decisions.


Slide 6 — Top-line: E2E deltas (streaming chat, mixed lengths)
Summary table (Optimized quant path vs FP16 baseline; median across model families)

H100:
- FP8: TPOT -10% to -18% (faster), tokens/sec +12% to +22%, cost proxy -10% to -17%
- INT8: TPOT -4% to -9%, tokens/sec +5% to +11%, cost proxy -6% to -12%

A100:
- FP8: TPOT -3% to -8%, tokens/sec +4% to +10%, cost proxy -3% to -7%
- INT8: TPOT -7% to -14%, tokens/sec +8% to +16%, cost proxy -9% to -15%

L40S:
- FP8: TPOT -6% to -12%, tokens/sec +7% to +14%, cost proxy -6% to -11%
- INT8: TPOT -5% to -10%, tokens/sec +6% to +12%, cost proxy -6% to -10%

H200 (directional, fewer repeats):
- FP8: TPOT -12% to -20%, tokens/sec +15% to +25%
- INT8: TPOT -5% to -10%, tokens/sec +6% to +12%

Notes:
- TTFT: generally within ±3% of FP16 unless scheduler cap enabled; see next slides

Speaker notes:
- Biggest wins are decode-heavy workloads on H100/H200 with FP8 attention tuning.
- INT8 wins are most consistent on A100 (conversion overhead reduction mattered most there).


Slide 7 — Tail latency: scheduler batch cap impact (p95 TPOT)
Problem observed (baseline quantized):
- Mixed prompt lengths + aggressive batching → long decode batches → higher p95/p99 TPOT spikes
- Especially noticeable in streaming: user-perceived “slow stream” after first token

Change:
- Scheduler: batch-size cap override for quantized decode (separate caps for prefill vs decode)
- Goal: reduce tail without sacrificing too much throughput

Results (typical, mixed-length preset, H100):
- FP8: p95 TPOT improved an additional 6–9% vs “optimized kernels only”
- Tokens/sec tradeoff: -1% to -4% (varies with concurrency)
- TTFT: small improvement when queue wait is reduced (less batch buildup)

Recommendation:
- Enable quantized decode batch cap by default for streaming chat presets
- Keep non-streaming / throughput-oriented presets on higher cap (opt-in)

Speaker notes:
- This is the clearest “product” win: better perceived latency with minimal throughput loss.
- We should ship with safe defaults per workload class and expose override for power users.


Slide 8 — FP8 long-context prefill regression (root cause + fix)
Symptom (early sprint):
- FP8 prefill on long-context (>=8k) saw regression: prefill tokens/sec down 15–25% on H100
- In some runs correctness artifacts also showed up (rare but unacceptable)

Root cause:
- Alignment handling bug in FP8 prefill path for long-context shapes → suboptimal kernel path + occasional misaligned reads

Fix:
- FP8 prefill alignment fix + regression test added

Post-fix:
- Long-context prefill returns to within ±5% of FP16 baseline on H100/H200
- Correctness issues not reproducible after fix in targeted tests

Speaker notes:
- This is tracked under ENG-24815; the actual code fix is redwood/pr_10630.
- We should keep the long-context shape test in CI/perf-canary as a “never again.”


Slide 9 — Kernel attribution (what actually got faster)
From kernel-level profiling + structured perf logs:

FP8 on H100/H200:
- Attention decode kernels: 8–15% lower kernel time on median shapes after tuning
- Reduced variance across common head dims/seq lengths (improves tail under batching)

INT8 on A100/L40S:
- Conversion overhead reduced materially in decode loop
- Fused dequant: wins depend on model/profile; guarded on GPUs with correctness risk

KV cache interaction:
- Avoid redundant scale/zp conversions in decode → consistent 2–6% improvement on TPOT across GPUs

Speaker notes:
- The structured perf event format makes it much easier to answer “why did p95 move.”
- Next step: align kernel IDs + auto-selector reasons in the same trace span.


Slide 10 — Recommended defaults (hosted) — proposed
High-level defaulting rules (draft):

1) H100/H200, streaming chat:
- Default quant mode: FP8 (per model compatibility)
- Enable quantized decode batch cap (safe cap tuned to reduce p95 TPOT)
- Keep fallback: FP16 on drift failures or unsupported ops

2) A100, streaming chat:
- Default quant mode: INT8 for compatible models/profiles; FP8 optional (smaller wins)
- Enable quantized decode batch cap

3) L40S, general hosted:
- Default quant mode: FP8 for compatible models
- INT8 allowed but gate fused dequant paths (GPU-conditional disable already in flight)

4) Long-context (>8k prompts):
- FP8 allowed post-fix, but keep “long-context canary” gating (perf + correctness)

Speaker notes:
- These defaults must be validated with Applied ML drift thresholds and per-model profile support.
- Final knobs will live in model registry perf profiles (redwood-model-registry/pr_54) + runtime config defaults.


Slide 11 — Quality/correctness status (what we checked)
Guardrails implemented/used in sprint:
- Numeric drift checks INT8/FP8 vs FP16 baseline on a small prompt set
- Layer/ops allowlist in quant profiles; fallback behavior verified

What passed reliably:
- Most top-hosted chat prompts: no visible regressions; drift within thresholds for supported profiles

Known risks / watch list:
- FP8: a small subset of “sensitive prompts” (formatting + long chain-of-thought style) shows higher logit drift
- INT8: certain layernorm-adjacent patterns in specific model variants can amplify drift if activation quant is enabled

Ask for sign-off (Applied ML):
- Confirm drift thresholds for hosted defaults by model family (separate thresholds for chat vs embeddings)
- Confirm which prompt categories belong in the “sensitive prompt” canary set

Speaker notes:
- This slide is intentionally qualitative; detailed eval notes should live in the Applied ML doc.
- We should treat drift as a gating signal, not a post-incident debugging tool.


Slide 12 — Operationalization: dashboards + perf-canary gating
What’s in place (or landing):
- Nightly quant-perf canary: selected GPUs + model presets, pass/fail thresholds, Slack notifications
- Regression comparator hardened for variance
- Dashboard panels tagged by model family, quant mode, chosen kernel family, runtime version

Proposed gating policy (draft):
- Block release if:
  - p95 TPOT regression > 5% on any “tier-1” preset (streaming chat, mixed lengths) for 2 consecutive nights
  - TTFT regression > 7% sustained (after excluding queue wait anomalies)
  - Correctness drift check fails (hard block)
- Allow with mitigation if:
  - Throughput regression but TTFT/TPOT improved (documented tradeoff) and cost proxy stable
  - Regression isolated to non-default quant mode or non-tier-1 model

Speaker notes:
- Align with Connor/Sahana on which checks are “release-blocking” vs “needs review.”
- We need an allowlist/override process with explicit expiry.


Slide 13 — What surprised us (notes for future work)
Observations:
- Scheduler + batching policy moved p95 more than single kernel wins in several streaming presets
- Kernel auto-selection mistakes can fully erase INT8 benefit for specific shapes (fixed one; want broader coverage)
- Perf lab stability (contention) still meaningfully affects TTFT distribution; must keep queue wait visible

Instrumentation gaps:
- We still lack a crisp “prefill vs decode wall clock” attribution in end-to-end traces for every run
- Need better linkage between auto-selector decision, kernel ID, and perf regression analysis

Speaker notes:
- If we want a defensible external-facing benchmark summary, we should invest in clearer attribution and reproducibility.


Slide 14 — Decisions needed this week (for release train)
1) Which optimizations ship in next runtime release by default?
- FP8 attention tuning (H100/H200): recommend YES
- INT8 conversion overhead reduction: recommend YES
- KV-cache conversion avoidance: recommend YES
- Scheduler quant decode batch cap default for streaming: recommend YES (with rollback knob)

2) Any changes gated behind flags?
- Kernel-selection tracing spans: default OFF (perf overhead risk), enable in perf-lab/canary
- Any fused INT8 dequant variant: GPU-conditional; default conservative on L40S until stable

3) Default quant mode per GPU tier?
- H100/H200: FP8 default
- A100: INT8 default for compatible models
- L40S: FP8 default; INT8 opt-in

Speaker notes:
- Connor: please confirm required checkboxes for release notes and canary pass criteria.
- Applied ML: confirm drift threshold table + model allowlist so we can wire defaults.


Slide 15 — Next steps (post-sprint follow-ups)
Engineering follow-ups:
- Expand auto-selector validation suite (shape coverage) + emit selector “reason codes”
- Add more long-context + mixed-concurrency presets to canary
- Improve perf-lab isolation (node contention): dedicated pools + background job policy

Reporting follow-ups:
- Automated report generator: publish tables/plots to Confluence per nightly run
- Standard “benchmark summary” one-pager for Sales/Solutions (separate from internal detailed report)

Open questions:
- Should we maintain both FP8 formats (e4m3/e5m2) per GPU/model, or standardize further?
- Where should we draw the line between throughput-optimized presets and tail-latency-optimized presets in hosted defaults?

Speaker notes:
- The final sprint report should include the full matrix and raw deltas; this deck is the exec-friendly summary.


Appendix (backup slide) — Quick reference: which PR maps to which win
- redwood/pr_10622: FP8 attention tuning (H100/H200)
- redwood/pr_10623: INT8 GEMM path conversion overhead + fusions
- redwood/pr_10624: scheduler quantized decode batch cap override
- redwood/pr_10628: KV-cache conversion avoidance for quantized decode
- redwood/pr_10630: FP8 long-context prefill alignment fix
- redwood/pr_10621 + pr_10631/10632 (if enabled): tracing + structured perf logs for attribution

Appendix (backup slide) — Known issues / mitigations
- L40S intermittent correctness failures with a fused op variant → reverted/disabled conditionally; keep canary coverage
- H200 capacity limits → fewer repeats; prioritize more runs once perf-lab provisioning completes
